newsitem.title: USA: Liability critical issue in tobacco talks.
newsitem.headline: Liability critical issue in tobacco talks.

text.p: Settlement talks between state attorneys general and the tobacco industry were at a pivotal point with liability being the critical issue, one of the negotiators said Wednesday.

"Liability is the critical issue," Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal said during a break in talks among the attorneys general, who met separately Wednesday morning before meeting tobacco representatives in the afternoon.
Blumenthal said while the two sides had made progress in their landmark talks, they were still far apart.
"We have reached a pivotal point in the negotiations," he said.
While he still had hope of reaching an agreement, Blumenthal said he would not put odds of obtaining a settlement above "50-50."

Blumenthal said the attorneys general had made proposals to cigarette companies that would allow them to anticipate their potential financial liability without depriving plaintiffs of their right to sue.
"There is a real possibility of securing a high degree of predictability through the ideas we have put on the table," Blumenthal said. He declined to give details.

Another negotiator, however, told Reuters previously that one idea would allow plaintiffs to sue cigarette companies and any damages awarded would be paid out of a special fund with an annual cap. If the fund is exhausted in one year, a successful plaintiff would get paid the following year.
The attorneys general were united in their stance that they will not agree to a settlement that would give the industry total protection from lawsuits, Blumenthal said.
He said the attorneys general were determined to preserve individuals' right to sue cigarette makers.
"If they are insisting on taking away a person's rights, then the chances of settlement are significantly diminished," Blumenthal said.

The attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. Also taking part in the negotiations are members of the health community and lawyers representing smokers and their families.
Although none of the attorneys general would give details on the discussions, they said that they decided to continue talks with the industry on Wednesday because they felt progress was being made.

The attorneys general also indicated Wednesday that they had rejected an industry plan that would set stiff barriers for smokers seeking compensation from the industry, capping claims at $250,000 and barring punitive damages.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore said that proposal, which was reported in Wednesday's Wall Street Journal, was "old news" and that the negotiators were "way beyond that."
